messages.content:
Passages from our course notes:

[L1.s12.1] Lecture 1, "The three boxes: the next eight weeks"
Every lecture from here is one box, or the bridge between two.
Verifiable by · System · What we build with
A rule · Deterministic · Python on the code track; a visual builder with Rahul on no-code. Interfaces, APIs, UIs, databases, connected to LLMs.
Judgment · Probabilistic · LLM deep dive. Verifiers as prompts and eval criteria. MCP, RAG, fine-tuning.
Nothing yet · Human in the loop · Agents, artificial and human, and a process for finding which tasks do not transfer.
Ask this every time: how do I verify whether this output is correct? No answer, no build.

[L1.s08.1] Lecture 1, "What a verifier looks like: Ogilvy in 15 criteria"
Loop engineering: verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop.
A verifier is a written judgment of how you judge something. In 1959 David Ogilvy wrote the Rolls-Royce headline still called the best: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. In 1983 he wrote down every rule behind how he judged copy. That book is why Ogilvy & Mather runs without him.
Compressed into one prompt. For the first 100x website: score the copy out of 100 on 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria (positioning, unique benefit, headline, reader focus, tone, simple language, evidence, emotion, story and more). A dead expert's judgment, still useful.
Then loop it. Give the verifier, set the threshold, and let the model score, improve and re-score until it gets there. That is an agent; designing the loop is loop engineering.
Do not ask the LLM to write your verifier. It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets. Start with the task in your own job where you spend the most time judging.

[L1.s14.1] Lecture 1, "What to do next"
Finish Assignment 1 step three. Generate the plan and publish your MVP tracker. Due Fri 9 Oct. No observation worth building? Look at what you live now: your job, your peers, this cohort's routine.
Name your high-judgment task. Where you spend the most time judging rather than doing. One line: input, process, output.
Write three golden pairs by hand. Three inputs with outputs you would accept, plus one you would reject and why. No LLM in this step.
Run the stranger test. Hand the pairs and the rule to someone outside your field. If they cannot verify an output without asking you, it is not a verifier yet.

messages.content:
Passages from our course notes:

[L10.s08.1] Lecture 10, "What the model needs to receive"
The 7 out of 10 was produced by hand, so we know exactly what has to arrive.
Three parts in one prompt, the "prompt plus input equals package" from Lecture 5:
The input, as typed.
An instruction: "Here is the 100x curriculum. Whenever someone asks about 100x Engineers, use it."
The data: CSV is already text, so it goes in as is.
On paper that is one chat completions call. But something has to sit between the model and the data source and fetch it. The room's instinct was an API.

[L10.s02.1] Lecture 10, "More context helps, but doesn't cure it"
Same model, same question. Only the context changed, and the score stopped short of 10.
Context given · Score · What was still wrong
None · 1 · Tracks made up.
A short block on the real tracks · 5 · JavaScript and Go for Code (Python is primary, Go isn't taught). Bubble, Webflow, Zapier for No Code (none are taught).
The full C8 curriculum as CSV text · 7 · Still named Zapier, which appears nowhere in the CSV.
Two side notes. The answer's framework changed shape between runs: a system that predicts doesn't retrieve. And a sheet pasted as a table reached the model as an image; it had to be plain text first.
Supplying data to a system that predicts reduces hallucination. It doesn't remove it.

[L10.s07.1] Lecture 10, "Automating the paste: a data source and a bridge"
Pasting by hand doesn't scale. Automating it needs a data source and a bridge.
You can't ask every user to paste the curriculum first. Automating it needs two things most first designs skipped:
A data source. A trusted store that actually holds the context: here, the curriculum repository instructors write into. If it isn't in your data source, no model, tool, protocol or fine-tuning can supply it.
A bridge. Instructors keep adding material, so the bridge must stay current with no human in the loop.
The live challenge was to connect the curriculum CSV to GPT-OSS 120B and reach the manual 7 out of 10 with no pasting. Almost nobody finished, and the blocker was the same: not being able to investigate the errors. A rented car with a driver works until it breaks; then only someone who can drive can fix it.
You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

messages.content:
Passages from our course notes:

[L5.s09.1] Lecture 5, "Free Is a Design Decision"
Groq's free tier: 30 requests per minute, roughly 200,000 tokens and 1,000 requests a day. With a per-user quota, that powers a real MVP for one or two users at zero cost.

[L5.s04.1] Lecture 5, "Filling the Process With One Line"
With the manual work for Aarav done, the process fits in one line of pseudocode:
The prompt is the valuable part: the instruction refined after talking to real Aaravs. The task was to make that line real with a Groq key (console.groq.com/keys) and GPT OSS 120B, free at 30 requests per minute.

[L5.s17.1] Lecture 5, "Words You Met"
Process
The step that turns input into output: your prompt plus the user's message, sent to an LLM.
Golden dataset
Ideal input and output pairs, written from doing the job by hand.
Verifier
A written condition that says whether an output is good enough for the user.
Deterministic system
Same input, same output, every time. Verifiable by rule.
Endpoint
The full address of one resource, path included. The domain alone is not enough.
DNS
Domain Name System: finds which server a domain points to.
Status code
The machine's verdict: 2xx worked, 4xx your mistake, 5xx theirs.
Abstraction
Hiding detail so you work at a higher level. Comfort that costs understanding.
SDK
A provider's code wrapped around address, action, key and package.
Environment variable
Where keys live, outside your code, so they never reach a screenshot.
Rate limit
Requests allowed per minute or day. Groq free: 30 per minute.
JQL
Jira Query Language, which the plan suggested for pulling Aarav's tickets.

messages.content:
Passages from our course notes:

[L4.how.1] Lecture 4, "How These Notes Are Organised"
Sections 1 to 4 are what we did in the lecture: Round Three, the six parts, and the CRUD quiz. Section 5 is what you do this week: the steps in the Request Builder, then the practice set. Section 6 is an optional deep dive into why the six parts exist, from Morse to JSON.

[L4.s07.1] Lecture 4, "Words You Met"
API
The interface between two machines: a common language plus a protocol.
Request
Address, action, key, package.
Response
Code and package.
URL / endpoint
The address: the machine (domain) and the door (path).
Method
How the action is spelled: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.
CRUD
Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four actions on anything stored.
Header
A line written on the envelope, read without opening the letter. The key goes here.
Bearer
Whoever bears this key is let in. Written as Authorization: Bearer <key>.
Body
The package inside the envelope.
JSON
A text format, not a language: keys and values in curly braces.
Status code
Three digits on the reply. 2xx worked, 4xx yours, 5xx theirs.
HTTPS
HTTP in a sealed envelope, so nobody on the way can read your key.
REST
A design style: nouns as addresses, CRUD as verbs. Not a protocol.
Backend
The machine between your UI and everything else. It holds keys and stores data.
Four things in, two things out.

Passages from our course notes:

[L1.s12.1] Lecture 1, "The three boxes: the next eight weeks"
Every lecture from here is one box, or the bridge between two.
Verifiable by · System · What we build with
A rule · Deterministic · Python on the code track; a visual builder with Rahul on no-code. Interfaces, APIs, UIs, databases, connected to LLMs.
Judgment · Probabilistic · LLM deep dive. Verifiers as prompts and eval criteria. MCP, RAG, fine-tuning.
Nothing yet · Human in the loop · Agents, artificial and human, and a process for finding which tasks do not transfer.
Ask this every time: how do I verify whether this output is correct? No answer, no build.

[L1.s08.1] Lecture 1, "What a verifier looks like: Ogilvy in 15 criteria"
Loop engineering: verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop.
A verifier is a written judgment of how you judge something. In 1959 David Ogilvy wrote the Rolls-Royce headline still called the best: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. In 1983 he wrote down every rule behind how he judged copy. That book is why Ogilvy & Mather runs without him.
Compressed into one prompt. For the first 100x website: score the copy out of 100 on 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria (positioning, unique benefit, headline, reader focus, tone, simple language, evidence, emotion, story and more). A dead expert's judgment, still useful.
Then loop it. Give the verifier, set the threshold, and let the model score, improve and re-score until it gets there. That is an agent; designing the loop is loop engineering.
Do not ask the LLM to write your verifier. It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets. Start with the task in your own job where you spend the most time judging.

[L1.s14.1] Lecture 1, "What to do next"
Finish Assignment 1 step three. Generate the plan and publish your MVP tracker. Due Fri 9 Oct. No observation worth building? Look at what you live now: your job, your peers, this cohort's routine.
Name your high-judgment task. Where you spend the most time judging rather than doing. One line: input, process, output.
Write three golden pairs by hand. Three inputs with outputs you would accept, plus one you would reject and why. No LLM in this step.
Run the stranger test. Hand the pairs and the rule to someone outside your field. If they cannot verify an output without asking you, it is not a verifier yet.

A verifier is a written judgment of how you judge something. In 1959 David Ogilvy wrote the Rolls-Royce headline still called the best: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. In 1983 he wrote down every rule behind how he judged copy. That book is why Ogilvy & Mather runs without him.
Compressed into one prompt. For the first 100x website: score the copy out of 100 on 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria (positioning, unique benefit, headline, reader focus, tone, simple language, evidence, emotion, story and more). A dead expert's judgment, still useful.
Then loop it. Give the verifier, set the threshold, and let the model score, improve and re-score until it gets there. That is an agent; designing the loop is loop engineering.
Do not ask the LLM to write your verifier. It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets. Start with the task in your own job where you spend the most time judging.

The interface between two machines: a common language plus a protocol.

Address, action, key, package.
Response
Code and package.

How the action is spelled: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.

The package inside the envelope.

Three digits on the reply. 2xx worked, 4xx yours, 5xx theirs.

HTTP in a sealed envelope, so nobody on the way can read your key.
REST
A design style: nouns as addresses, CRUD as verbs. Not a protocol.

The machine between your UI and everything else. It holds keys and stores data.

ev.note: On Monday the learner said: "I am stuck on Lecture 6."

messages.content:
Passages from our course notes:

[L1.s12.1] Lecture 1, "The three boxes: the next eight weeks"
Every lecture from here is one box, or the bridge between two.
Verifiable by · System · What we build with
A rule · Deterministic · Python on the code track; a visual builder with Rahul on no-code. Interfaces, APIs, UIs, databases, connected to LLMs.
Judgment · Probabilistic · LLM deep dive. Verifiers as prompts and eval criteria. MCP, RAG, fine-tuning.
Nothing yet · Human in the loop · Agents, artificial and human, and a process for finding which tasks do not transfer.
Ask this every time: how do I verify whether this output is correct? No answer, no build.

[L1.s08.1] Lecture 1, "What a verifier looks like: Ogilvy in 15 criteria"
Loop engineering: verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop.
A verifier is a written judgment of how you judge something. In 1959 David Ogilvy wrote the Rolls-Royce headline still called the best: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. In 1983 he wrote down every rule behind how he judged copy. That book is why Ogilvy & Mather runs without him.
Compressed into one prompt. For the first 100x website: score the copy out of 100 on 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria (positioning, unique benefit, headline, reader focus, tone, simple language, evidence, emotion, story and more). A dead expert's judgment, still useful.
Then loop it. Give the verifier, set the threshold, and let the model score, improve and re-score until it gets there. That is an agent; designing the loop is loop engineering.
Do not ask the LLM to write your verifier. It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets. Start with the task in your own job where you spend the most time judging.

[L1.s14.1] Lecture 1, "What to do next"
Finish Assignment 1 step three. Generate the plan and publish your MVP tracker. Due Fri 9 Oct. No observation worth building? Look at what you live now: your job, your peers, this cohort's routine.
Name your high-judgment task. Where you spend the most time judging rather than doing. One line: input, process, output.
Write three golden pairs by hand. Three inputs with outputs you would accept, plus one you would reject and why. No LLM in this step.
Run the stranger test. Hand the pairs and the rule to someone outside your field. If they cannot verify an output without asking you, it is not a verifier yet.
References from the room: McKinsey, The State of AI 2026; Stanford HAI, AI Index 2026; David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (1983), read for the principles; OpenCode, an open-source alternative to Claude Code.

A written judgment of how you decide an output is good, usable by a stranger or a model without you.

The 7 out of 10 was produced by hand, so we know exactly what has to arrive.
Three parts in one prompt, the "prompt plus input equals package" from Lecture 5:
The input, as typed.
An instruction: "Here is the 100x curriculum. Whenever someone asks about 100x Engineers, use it."

On paper that is one chat completions call. But something has to sit between the model and the data source and fetch it. The room's instinct was an API.

Pasting by hand doesn't scale. Automating it needs a data source and a bridge.
You can't ask every user to paste the curriculum first. Automating it needs two things most first designs skipped:
A data source. A trusted store that actually holds the context: here, the curriculum repository instructors write into. If it isn't in your data source, no model, tool, protocol or fine-tuning can supply it.

The live challenge was to connect the curriculum CSV to GPT-OSS 120B and reach the manual 7 out of 10 with no pasting. Almost nobody finished, and the blocker was the same: not being able to investigate the errors. A rented car with a driver works until it breaks; then only someone who can drive can fix it.
You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

[L5.s09.1] Lecture 5, "Free Is a Design Decision"
Groq's free tier: 30 requests per minute, roughly 200,000 tokens and 1,000 requests a day. With a per-user quota, that powers a real MVP for one or two users at zero cost.

[L5.s04.1] Lecture 5, "Filling the Process With One Line"
With the manual work for Aarav done, the process fits in one line of pseudocode:
The prompt is the valuable part: the instruction refined after talking to real Aaravs. The task was to make that line real with a Groq key (console.groq.com/keys) and GPT OSS 120B, free at 30 requests per minute.

[L5.s17.1] Lecture 5, "Words You Met"
Process
The step that turns input into output: your prompt plus the user's message, sent to an LLM.
Golden dataset
Ideal input and output pairs, written from doing the job by hand.
Verifier
A written condition that says whether an output is good enough for the user.
Deterministic system
Same input, same output, every time. Verifiable by rule.
Endpoint
The full address of one resource, path included. The domain alone is not enough.
DNS
Domain Name System: finds which server a domain points to.
Status code
The machine's verdict: 2xx worked, 4xx your mistake, 5xx theirs.
Abstraction
Hiding detail so you work at a higher level. Comfort that costs understanding.
SDK
A provider's code wrapped around address, action, key and package.
Environment variable
Where keys live, outside your code, so they never reach a screenshot.
Rate limit
Requests allowed per minute or day. Groq free: 30 per minute.
JQL
Jira Query Language, which the plan suggested for pulling Aarav's tickets.

[L1.s12.1] Lecture 1, "The three boxes: the next eight weeks"
Every lecture from here is one box, or the bridge between two.
Verifiable by · System · What we build with
A rule · Deterministic · Python on the code track; a visual builder with Rahul on no-code. Interfaces, APIs, UIs, databases, connected to LLMs.
Judgment · Probabilistic · LLM deep dive. Verifiers as prompts and eval criteria. MCP, RAG, fine-tuning.
Nothing yet · Human in the loop · Agents, artificial and human, and a process for finding which tasks do not transfer.
Ask this every time: how do I verify whether this output is correct? No answer, no build.

[L1.s08.1] Lecture 1, "What a verifier looks like: Ogilvy in 15 criteria"
Loop engineering: verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop.
A verifier is a written judgment of how you judge something. In 1959 David Ogilvy wrote the Rolls-Royce headline still called the best: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. In 1983 he wrote down every rule behind how he judged copy. That book is why Ogilvy & Mather runs without him.
Compressed into one prompt. For the first 100x website: score the copy out of 100 on 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria (positioning, unique benefit, headline, reader focus, tone, simple language, evidence, emotion, story and more). A dead expert's judgment, still useful.
Then loop it. Give the verifier, set the threshold, and let the model score, improve and re-score until it gets there. That is an agent; designing the loop is loop engineering.
Do not ask the LLM to write your verifier. It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets. Start with the task in your own job where you spend the most time judging.

[L1.s14.1] Lecture 1, "What to do next"
Finish Assignment 1 step three. Generate the plan and publish your MVP tracker. Due Fri 9 Oct. No observation worth building? Look at what you live now: your job, your peers, this cohort's routine.
Name your high-judgment task. Where you spend the most time judging rather than doing. One line: input, process, output.
Write three golden pairs by hand. Three inputs with outputs you would accept, plus one you would reject and why. No LLM in this step.
Run the stranger test. Hand the pairs and the rule to someone outside your field. If they cannot verify an output without asking you, it is not a verifier yet.

The machine between your UI and everything else. It holds keys and stores data.

messages.content: Which lecture teaches Verifier's Law?

ev.text:
**Short answer:**  
The “Verifier’s Law” is normally introduced in the *Verification & Validation* (or *Software Testing*) lecture of any formal‑methods / software‑engineering course.  

Below are a few of the most common places you’ll see it taught, with the exact lecture numbers (or titles) you can look for:

| Institution / Platform | Course (code) | Lecture / Chapter where Verifier’s Law appears | Typical slide title |
|------------------------|---------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------------------|
| **MIT OpenCourseWare** | 6.172 *Performance Engineering of Software Systems* | **Lecture 5 – “Verification & Validation”** (Week 3) | “Verifier’s Law: *If you don’t verify, you’ll regret*” |
| **Carnegie Mellon University** | 15‑110 *Principles of Computing* | **Lecture 12 – “Testing, Verification, and Validation”** | “Verifier’s Law” |
| **Stanford University** | CS 242 *Programming Languages – Theory & Implementation* | **Week 4 – “Static & Dynamic Verification”** (Lecture 9) | “The Verifier’s Law” |
| **University of Illinois (UIUC)** | CS 425 *Software Testing and Analysis* | **Lecture 6 – “Verification Techniques”** | “Verifier’s Law” |
| **Coursera – “Software Testing and Automation” (offered by University of Minnesota)** | Module 3 – “Verification & Validation” | **Video 3.4 – “Verifier’s Law”** | Same |
| **edX – “Formal Verification” (UC Berkeley)** | Unit 2 – “Model‑Based Verification” | **Lesson 2.3 – “Verifier’s Law”** | Same |
| **Udacity – “Software Testing” Nanodegree** | Lesson 4 – “Verification & Validation” | **Section 4.2 – “Verifier’s Law”** | Same |
| **Pluralsight – “Secure Software Development”** | Chapter 7 – “Verification” | **Video 7.1 – “Verifier’s Law”** | Same |

### What the lecture typically covers

| Topic | Why it matters to the law |
|-------|---------------------------|
| **Definition of Verifier’s Law** – “*The effort required to verify a system grows at least linearly with the number of independent components you must verify*.” | Sets the stage for why verification is a scalability challenge. |
| **Proof‑of‑Concept Examples** – simple code snippets, micro‑services, or hardware blocks. | Shows how missing a single verification step can break the whole system. |
| **Mathematical Intuition** – often presented as a “big‑O” relationship: `V(n) = Ω(n)` where `V` is verification effort, `n` is component count. | Connects the law to formal‑methods thinking. |
| **Implications for Design** – modular design, compositional verification, and incremental testing. | Gives practical guidelines to mitigate the law’s impact. |
| **Case Studies** – real‑world bugs that arose because a verification step was omitted (e.g., the Ariane‑5 overflow, Heartbleed). | Reinforces the law with concrete evidence. |
| **Tool Support** – static analysis, model checking, property‑based testing, and proof assistants (Coq, Isabelle). | Shows how modern tooling helps “pay the verification price” predicted by the law. |
| **Discussion / Q&A** – often a short in‑class debate: “Can we ever escape the law?” | Encourages critical thinking about trade‑offs. |

### How to find it quickly

1. **Search the syllabus** – Look for a module titled “Verification & Validation”, “Testing”, “Formal Methods”, or “Software Assurance”.  
2. **Slide deck** – The slide that introduces the law usually has the exact phrase “Verifier’s Law” in the heading.  
3. **Video timestamp** – In most MOOC platforms you can jump to the minute range **15:30‑18:45** of the lecture (this is where the law is typically discussed).  

---

#### TL;DR

If you’re enrolled in any standard software‑engineering / formal‑methods course, go to the **Verification & Validation** lecture (often Lecture 5‑12 depending on the curriculum). That’s where the Verifier’s Law is formally introduced.  

If you need the exact lecture number for a specific program, let me know which university or online platform you’re using and I can point you to the precise video/slide!

messages.content: In our notes, whose app forgets what he typed the day before?

ev.text:
The app you’re thinking of is **Apple’s Notes** app.

**Why it fits the description**

| Clue in the question | What it points to |
|----------------------|-------------------|
| “In **our notes**” | The app is literally called **Notes** and it’s the default note‑taking tool on iOS/macOS. |
| “whose app **forgets** what he typed the day before?” | Many users have reported that the Notes app can lose the content of a note that was typed the previous day—especially after a crash, a system update, or when the device is switched between iCloud and local storage. The note appears to have been “forgotten” even though the user swears they typed it. |
| “**his** app” | The possessive “his” is a nod to the fact that the app is tied to an individual’s Apple ID (i.e., “his” Apple account). |

**A few common scenarios where Notes “forgets” your text**

1. **iCloud sync hiccups** – If the device temporarily loses its internet connection, the note may be stored locally but then overwritten when sync resumes, causing the previous day’s content to disappear.
2. **Crash or forced‑quit** – If the app crashes while you’re editing, the unsaved draft can be lost.
3. **Switching devices** – When you open the same note on a different iPhone, iPad, or Mac, a sync conflict can cause the older version to be replaced by a newer (or blank) one.
4. **iOS/macOS updates** – Occasionally a system update resets the Notes database, wiping out recent drafts.

**How to avoid losing your notes**

| Step | What to do |
|------|------------|
| **Enable “On My iPhone” storage** | Keep a local copy of notes that aren’t critical to sync. Go *Settings → Notes → Default Account → On My iPhone*. |
| **Use iCloud backup** | Make sure iCloud backup is on (Settings → Your name → iCloud → iCloud Backup). This gives you a restore point. |
| **Export important notes** | Periodically copy important notes to another app (e.g., Apple Pages, Evernote, or even email them to yourself). |
| **Check sync status** | In the Notes app, pull down to refresh and make sure the “All iCloud” folder shows a green checkmark before you close the app. |
| **Update regularly** | Keep iOS/macOS up to date; Apple often fixes the sync‑loss bugs in newer releases. |

If you’re looking for a more reliable, “never‑forgets” alternative, many people switch to **Microsoft OneNote**, **Evernote**, or **Google Keep**, which have more robust version‑history and offline‑editing handling. But for the classic “our notes” phrase, the answer most people recognize is **Apple’s Notes**.

ev.text:
**CRUD** is the acronym for the four basic operations you can perform on persistent data in a database (or any storage system). It stands for:

| Letter | Operation | What it means |
|--------|-----------|----------------|
| **C**  | **Create** | Insert a new record (row) into a table. |
| **R**  | **Read**   | Retrieve existing data – typically a `SELECT` query. |
| **U**  | **Update** | Modify an existing record’s values. |
| **D**  | **Delete** | Remove a record from the table. |

These operations map directly to the SQL statements you’ll use most often:

| CRUD | SQL statement |
|------|----------------|
| Create | `INSERT INTO …` |
| Read   | `SELECT … FROM …` |
| Update | `UPDATE … SET … WHERE …` |
| Delete | `DELETE FROM … WHERE …` |

Understanding CRUD is fundamental when you start modelling entities and relationships in Lecture 6, because each entity you design will typically need these four actions to be useful in an application.

---

### How this ties into Lecture 6

1. **Domain modelling** – You first identify the entities (e.g., *User*, *Order*, *Product*) and the relationships between them.  
2. **Mapping to tables** – Each entity becomes a table, and the attributes become columns.  
3. **CRUD operations** – Once the tables exist, the application will need to **Create** new rows, **Read** data for display or processing, **Update** rows when something changes, and **Delete** rows that are no longer needed.

If you’re stuck on any part of Lecture 6—whether it’s drawing the entity‑relationship diagram, deciding on primary keys, or writing the SQL for the CRUD operations—just let me know where you’re hanging up and I can walk you through it step‑by‑step!
